paragraphs: In terms of interaction, people … are no different at all from an LLM, and an LLM that isn't trying at all)

To feel this right now, talk to some deep experts in their domain who long ago forgot that someone might not have a PhD in their subject. They sincerely believe they knew it all from the cradle, and everyone else isn't worthy of that knowledge.
For the full effect you need to talk to them precisely about their domain. Some narrowly specialized coder-founders are perfect for this.

Talking to such a person, you have to think hard about how to phrase the question so that he can answer it even somewhat intelligibly. It takes 10 or more attempts at the apparatus) With each attempt the risk of silence in reply increases.
No wonder Steve Wozniaks need Steve Jobses, so that their business team has more than two autists and more clients than a couple of childhood friends who did well =)
Lately I talk a lot with people who, before my recent leap in development smarts, wouldn't have talked to me at all.

God, how hard it is to make them simply answer some important question directly and completely. From some of them I'm trying to buy something, but it's incredibly hard to do, because they can't open their mouths and tell me in detail how their … specifically performs its function, and without that there's no point in buying — a vicious circle.

And that's me entertaining them as best I can, while an ordinary client wants to BE entertained) And even if he's entertained long and thoroughly enough, he'll still think about whether to transfer the money.

I have no doubt that even with … vibe-coding, in a scalable product business I need a technical co-founder. Not only because without him you can't scale load quickly, but because there's no time to deal with technology if sales are flying — you have to fundraise and … all over the world on a business mission, which pairs … with silent staring into a terminal.
However, in my memory the absolute majority of technical founders avoid sales/marketing/business co-founders in every way. Most likely out of disrespect.

So they sit on their technically perfect projects with 100 unique visitors a month on the site (95 of which are crawler bots), and … over forks and stars on GitHub, which don't bring in a … of commission)

Separately, I have to compliment the leap in design. And it's not only UI, it's product design too. I think these things come as a package — you can't understand better, at the level of reasoning, how to arrange the pixels if you don't understand, at the level of reasoning, what those pixels do, for whom and why.

As some have gathered, I built my own agency management system, which includes a fully proprietary Instantly, developed by me from top to bottom, and a dozen other systems, big and small. All the DocuSigns, Intuits and other stuff a business needs.

The huge plus of reproducing all these things under your own hood is their native connectedness with each other and with the core of the business. It's one thing to link these systems via API, and quite another when they're linked by one codebase and one database from the start;)
So: the screenshot shows an elementary, typical mechanism for adding CSV files, which get parsed correctly and turned into a campaign's mailing list. That's what the system will hurl emails by.
Previously I had it built so you pick a CSV file on disk, and off it goes.
I asked 5.4 xhigh to study everything related to CSV and think creatively about edge cases — does our system's design support them.
As a result 5.4 made me raise first one eyebrow, then the other.
It figured out things that not every human thinks of, judging by every interface I know of that I paid money for over the years:
1) Maybe someday we'll want to find the original source on disk, and we'd better know what that file is called, so we can search by the original name

2) Files are uploaded one at a time, but that's inconvenient. Why not just drag-and-drop the whole batch of any size and queue them for processing, with the option not to wait for the results of that processing — everything further happens by itself server-side.
3) A notification lands in Telegram with data on how many contacts were loaded, how many were deduplicated, how many days' worth of contacts the campaign now has.
4) Every interactive element has an icon; hover over it and a whole article pops up describing exactly what will happen if you click, and what results to expect.

And it all looks such that I can't find fault with it. The processing itself is animated too — looks like, I dunno, something out of a game — it's clear what's happening, every step of progress is visually emphasized.
Hardcore stuff, imho;)
Another big jump forward. Reminder: it's been 3 weeks since the last jump)
It's funny to watch product managers these days =)
Most of them turned out to be unable to build … at all. And “most” isn't 80%, it's about 99.99%
Those who did start building something with vibe-coding somehow turned out to be unable to build useful things that anyone besides themselves needs =)
Meanwhile, for about ten years now they've been paid no less than coders, and definitely more than salespeople. All I hear from everywhere is product managers this, product managers that.
So they were being paid for a … they obviously don't know how to do? =)
Or remind me please, what is a product manager's job)))

And in general, for any technology, if you need to somehow extend the basic set of functions, google “awesome” + the name of the library or technology, and almost always you'll find a huge repository of curated solutions
There are people who just get it)
Once a week Maxim advises something that, out of nowhere, makes me start producing better-quality vibe-coding.
No wonder half the city fights over him when he decides to change jobs.

One time Maxim helped protect a huge TV star from an attempt on her life by her boyfriend, by hacking his computer) Imagine your surprise if you're a … trying to poison someone, and instead you end up behind bars because somebody hacked your computer? That guy's mom definitely wasn't lying when she said he was one of a kind)
I really hope I can get back to the Interviews soon, and Maxim will drop by and tell the story :D
Meanwhile, enjoy his tips along with me.
…… You could really do that? With the right skills and libraries an LLM produces quality better than most design elements of the most expensive websites.
I'm sure most people make this mistake and beg their Claudes and Codexes in words to draw “something …,” and get a pixelated … in profile.
Treat your model to a good LIBRARY. A well-fed model — a beautiful design!

Max Outreachtodayevich, a coder from birth, unexpectedly paid me a nice little compliment. We were poking at his API, and when I told him I'm a dumb … who can't get a certain list of features to fail-proof working order in two days, he let slip the phrase “Tim, you … underestimate yourself.”

Then he told me about the hundred interviews he'd conducted recently. They were looking for a couple of coders, but Max fully shares my worldview on the transformation of everything, and he needed coders who were exclusively AI-positive/native. In short, vibe-coders far more than coders.
He conducted a HUNDRED interviews, and it was a select hundred — he'd pre-screened many of them with tricky little questions.
And they couldn't hire anyone))

And the biggest idiocy is that he interviews a guy who, apparently with GPT's help, described how … of a vibe-coder he is, and tells him, okay, share your screen, show me what your setup looks like, how and what and why you prompt, and so on. In the end most people in March 2026 show that they … don't really know how to vibe-code at all.

Think about it: he asked a number of people to run a command in the terminal that showed the Cursor install date — 8 hours ago =)))) He did this when it was obvious the guy was on such formal terms with the interface of what he calls his main work machine that it was simply interesting to expose the degree of hidden ….

One guy, when Max caught him red-handed, just burst into tears like a little girl. He said it was all unfair, and he didn't want to retrain, he wanted the world to go back to when you could calmly … three scripts and get a big salary for ….

What I'd say to such a guy in Max's place I don't even know. I think I'd just press the red button. Not because I'm so … heartless, but because that dumbass is … heartless. I already work like a beast, pay everyone around me money, spin like a hamster in a wheel, and now some lazy … is going to flap air in front of me, squeezing time, dough, emotional support and energy out of me by every means, giving … back in return. Sit your … down and learn, it's even FREE, why the … are you messing with people's heads, you … :)))))))
In short, I have no time for anything right now except what I've been laboring on for … knows how many days now… 60?
But the brain wants at least some entertainment, at least in a neighboring development branch; it's not made of iron.
So in parallel I'm tinkering with my Ultima Online server. It's been Up And Running for a week, but I'm dressing it up with scripts that will make the game on this server special and unforgettable:)

The plus of Ultima is that you can play it by playing, or play it without playing (automations, leveling characters = something happens, there's progress, and you just see it out of the corner of your eye and feel happy).
Usually all shard owners consider automation cheating and fight it. They also believe that a shard's atmosphere and gameplay consist not of possibilities but of restrictions.

Like, let's make it so … isn't allowed. Let's make it so your stats are only enough to die in the forest to a bear. Let's make it so people don't have enough … for anything at all — that'll make the game so much more fun for them! Let's forbid them to mine ore automatically. Let's forbid them to hunt or do quests automatically. And if even after that one of these … succeeds, let's wipe the … server))))
I'm not that kind of guy, of course. I want to build an Ultima shard designed for a world where vibe-coding exists and people have jobs and businesses =)
I want to make leveling hard to automate and, correspondingly, practically impossible to play by hand.

All restrictions go in the …. Any character can be maxed out in every skill. Crafting is built so that if you don't automate resource gathering and defense against monsters and other players along the way — nobody … needs you on this shard, go play on Outlands, they'll humiliate you there before you even register, and then every minute after)
I want to make not the game hard, but the world around it, which you'll still have to manage to cope with despite all of modern AI playing on your side;)
And the AI there will have to play not only for us but against us. I want to build an AI for the dragons and other beasts such that dealing with them is, to put it mildly, not easy =)
Raid bosses will have to be raided by hand, simply because I can hardly imagine an automation that could cope with the mechanics I've dreamed up. It'll take true …, and for that you go to humans :D
And of course it'll run on a MacBook, on mobile, in the browser, not just on Windows like all the wretched shards made by tram-depot administrators for tax-office clerks.
And for donations you'll be able to buy whole cities if you like =)))
Skill boosts, weapons of unheard-of power, etc. I never understood the point of no-donations or cosmetics-only shards.

If I want to buy myself a meteorite club for a grand and go around … everyone with it — why not?!?!!??!??!!?!?!??!? None of those admins was ever able to answer that question for me. They only came up with NO, but didn't bother to come up with a WHY for each NO. That's hard, after all)

I want to record this strange moment here. Someday I'll want to reread how this becoming-a-vibe-coder happened, and it'll be nice to remember that on March 13, 2026, I sank to the point where in ~28 hours from the moment my tokens were reset I burned through more than 50% of the weekly limit on the PRO subscription for GPT 5.4 — even though I don't use the speed boost that eats 2x, and I set the model's context to 500k, where the first 275k go without doubling, and I have to admit I don't very often exceed 275k in a single task, and I very rarely run two tasks on one context.

Not long ago it seemed to me that burning through the Pro plan by hand was simply impossible. It also seemed to me that developing a project would never need more than one file, and 8k lines was a lot.

After the latest refactor I reduced the number of files in ONE OF FOUR REPOS to 437 from about 548, and there's less code there. Only 200 thousand lines versus 350k, not counting tests (1,300 of them in 128 files)..
Curious what comes next =)
Guys, imagine — I … hadn't noticed that GPT has a GitHub connector.

And I noticed it because I'd started missing GPT 5.2 PRO, which so nicely helped me think through the deep architecture of important pieces of the system, where Codex itself seemed to lack the time OpenAI lets it think.
I'd usually throw an archive of the project into 5.2 PRO, wait an hour, and get a very well-thought-out prompt for Codex, much stronger than what plan mode in Codex can do.

However, when my repo outgrew 50k lines of code, GPT 5.2 PRO started throwing an error on an archive context of that size, and I realized that from there on Codex and I were left alone, and Pro could no longer help us at the global level.

Right now my repo has about 155 thousand lines, and I decided to try whether anything had changed in 5.4 PRO, and O MIRACLE: 5.4 PRO happily swallowed the archive and … reviewed my entire 155-thousand-line project, not counting tests!!!
And then I saw the Git connector and got really happy.

I set up the connector, dropped a prompt without an archive, and it turned out that Pro loses the connector before it starts reasoning, can't find my private repo, tries to search for it on the Internet and doesn't see it because it's Private.
I was upset, but for the sake of experiment asked 5.3 instant to look at the repo through the connector… and it saw it. The connector didn't drop.
Then I asked 5.4 thinking.
It also saw the connector and my private repo.
Went back to PRO, and this … once again doesn't see my repo …!!!!!!!!!!!!!
So the most useful model is the only one that drops my GitHub connector and can't reason over the repo for me.
Meanwhile it reasons over a zip archive of the repo just fine.
Is this a known bug? Is it a … paid feature? What the … is this, does anyone understand?
Dropping a zip isn't God knows what kind of problem, but it's strange.

And the problem with the zip is that if you then throw a second prompt into the same window with a modified repo, it kills Pro's brain, since it sees both zips at once with different content and gets lost guessing which one is correct, and starts producing …. Restricting the reading to the second file only is useless; the first one still gets captured in the context, checked twice.
Halp
Okay, so who among us here are the Ultima connoisseurs and fans? Please throw into the chat, from your memories, what seems important to you and what you'd really miss. The more the better.

Between other things I've already built a lot; the server launch is very soon. I'm not going to … over it forever before launch, because afterwards we'll just polish it together based on your feedback.

The main thing I'm finishing now is my own hand-written Inject, which is simply built into the client and will allow any automations. Frankly, I'm even considering letting you just paste in a model's token and let it control the game with no automations at all =)

In that case you could say “Yo, can you please max out all my skills? By any means; if you're missing something to be more efficient — get it by doing the necessary intermediate actions.” Or “Run around Moonglow and … someone; if they get you, try to run away, and if that doesn't work I'll wipe you ….”

But I think that would be worse than scripting, because Ultima isn't just actions, it's also reaction speed to what's happening, and a script will probably pull a reaction out of the model in any case =)

Although tasks like “log into my Plevel 7 account and dress all the NPCs in the game in thoughtful, beautiful outfits, much richer than default, with colors matching the spirit of each city, etc. — come up with the accessories and all that … yourself” — the LLM does simply magnificently :D

In short, folks, as usual I'm getting fundamentally new experience through a game. Back in December I built chess, and thanks to that I learned interfaces, dynamic elements, traffic and much more, which I then wonderfully applied in my SalesBomb automation machine of 230 thousand lines (including tests and failsafes, as of today).
And now I'm doing something completely new for me — working not with the web over HTTP, but with a distribution, file libraries, a client being rewritten completely from scratch for my task.

So — it's … mesmerizing to watch Codex juggle files, test servers, builds. Every now and then new versions of the client open, Codex measures something, runs around a bit, clicks buttons in the game, hums disapprovingly, kills the process, goes and rewrites something, recompiles, assembles a new build, tests again. This goes on for hours. It works with a live file system significantly longer than with web services, and it runs simply … tons of tests that brought my computer to life. Some coder gizmos get installed, some programs restart, and a completely different reasoning monologue in the chat. It really digs around like a detective, openly rejoices at progress, gets upset that it crashed again…
Ferocious bliss)))
This kind of … happens regularly when you work with the file system.

But I understood why. An order of magnitude less context gets spent. It writes code for a while and the context flies away, but then when the file-system debugging starts, all those tests with launches, installations of all kinds of junk, restarts, builds-…, all of that consumes extremely little context. Context is measured not in gigabytes of files but in thousands of characters. And to check a status and send a terminal command takes a piddling number of characters.
And OpenAI apparently lets Codex do whatever its heart desires on low-token tasks. In those 2 hours 20 minutes, no joke, ~250k tokens were burned. Of which 200k in the first 25 minutes or so)
Guys, please don't forget the main thing: vibe-coders don't code.
Many write, like, I coded this up with Cursor, with Claude Code…
You did not …)
Real vibe-coders ASK.
Not coded, but ASKED FOR.
Not coding, but ASKING.
Some beg or aggressively demand, but those get bad, boorish vibe-code-code, because the LLM returns a result symmetrical to the request.
You have to be courteous with it. You have to ASK it, and then it does everything smoothly.
Right now I've ASKED my LLM to build me about three more hours' worth of vibe-coding features, while I'm running around the garden with a shovel replacing the lawn:)
Read this and many other valuable tips in this Telegram channel! And throw some dough my way for tokens so I can … generate even more tips for you:
Until March 18 I'm living on Codex credits, which are bought on top of the $200 subscription when the weekly limit is exceeded.
If you work on one project one prompt at a time, $5 flies away in about 1.5–2 hours of vibe-coding.

So 12 hours of very smooth work on ONE project a day will suck up about $25. If you work on 3 projects in parallel and have Codex do one-off … during the day, I think $100 will fly away too, without false modesty.
I'm not strong in math, but I … sense that credits are noticeably more expensive than the token limit in the body of the subscription))))

Although it's not even clear how to count the body of the subscription) There's so much in there. Deep research, all kinds of other modes, the Pro model, etc. If you count the subscription as containing the full $200 worth of Codex tokens — credits are still noticeably more expensive than the subscription bundle.
And if you count the Codex unit in the $200 subscription as a half or a quarter of the total subscription cost — then credits become simply astronomically expensive compared to the subscription body.

However, a couple of years ago Altman said an agent should cost a small business the same as one employee at 2–3 thousand dollars a month, while doing far more than an employee would for that money. Ideally doing absolutely everything =)
I think that's where they're heading, both to “doing absolutely everything” and to “2–3 thousand dollars” =)

I wonder — if you code with an API token, does it come out the same? Coding by token on frontier models seems even more expensive? Though my latest data is from March '25, when the Escalator staff, two of them, burned through … 20 thousand dollars in a month with Opus.
In general, as someone rightly noted recently in the discussion group, coding has rapidly moved from “you get paid for it” to “you pay for it” =)))

But guys, that's not because someone is trying to … coders, it's because it's not coders who code now. And before, these “non-coders” paid coders … knows how many hundreds of times more for development than they pay OpenAI, if you count the output per invested dollar =)

There's a lot more you could reason about here, of course. In particular, that everyone who busted their ass vibe-coding like me from September to March got a wonderful opportunity to learn practically for free.
From here on it will all get more and more expensive every quarter)
It can't be otherwise, unless of course Sam Altman invents a new economy and sells it to all of civilization, which I very much doubt :D
How do you like this art for the installer splash screen of the shard?:)
By the way, this shard has one feature: I do nothing by hand, and I mean ….

Every setting, every file, every monster, every piece of clothing, every button, every NPC, every corner of the map, every type of art in every city — all of it is done exclusively through the Codex APP.

In all this time I've logged into my own server 3 times: to test the mind-blowing new-school inject that Codex wrote, to play with the TypeScript scripts, and to poke around in the, again hand-written, GM control panel for the shard, for GMs if we ever have any)
It's kind of my gestalt — to make an AI-native UO shard that's steeped not only in a maximalist's Ultima but thoroughly steeped in AI, 360 degrees)

Just finished a smart updater that once a day will collect all the accumulated release candidates and push them to the updater. Characters will become invulnerable and lose connection, and you'll be able to come back through the triggered updater, like in Dota.

Crisis bugfixes will be force-pushed bypassing this, so at first it'll probably disconnect more often than once a day, but over time there'll be nothing left to polish on the client side, and server updates like new items don't need a client update, or even a server restart)
That's the little technical design =)
Part of this is dreamed up by GPT PRO, part by 5.4 in Codex. And all the rest by your lazy servant, who … doesn't want to do anything by hand, only code 14 hours a day …)
Don't forget the wish list in the discussion group, those who know what Ultima is and are waiting for the release)

The first 50 accounts will get … beautiful perks, some of them during the first 200 hours online;) The only thing you won't be able to do on autopilot on this shard is stand around doing nothing. Idling will disconnect you; disconnect for idling more than X times — IP ban) At least level hiding, for crying out loud;)
By the way, all of this in my life started happening when I began vibe-coding 24/7. I swear, discover round-the-clock vibe-coding, you won't regret it!!!

Vibe-coding is helped enormously by asking Codex, while it checks the results of its own work, to look with its eyes at what came out, instead of settling for a glance at the database and the assumption that it all renders correctly on the front end.

On the web, the Chrome DevTools MCP helps abundantly with this, and on the file system Codex figured out to ask me to share screen-recording permission for the Codex App and Terminal App, and now it slyly snaps pictures of the DMGs and clients it launches and checks the result for pixel-perfect correspondence with what it expects should be there. Result: -95% visual glitches. It catches almost everything itself, criticizes itself, and fixes it itself. If not on the third try, then on the fifth. Honestly I … care which try it is, as long as I get a decent final product without intervening =)
Well, dear vibe-coders, congratulate me or something — for the first time in my life I bought myself a real VPS at Hetzner, where I'll be crawling over from Railway, which I've finally outgrown:)
Codex is now setting all this up with a prompt the size of Jupiter, authored by Monsieur GPT PRO:)
Dudes, help me understand:
So I took a fat Hetzner cloud… Overall it's already gorgeous, and I can do what I want on it, and … will anyone else do it for me.

However, I want, for example, to run 3 different services on it. That's Ultima, and my private sender for 17 thousand mailboxes, and a couple of landing pages, and a Telegram bot, and the control panel for SLSBMB. Oops, that's not even 3 but … more.
Doesn't matter. What matters… What's the simplest and most straightforward way to do this? Why I'm asking:

You all understand perfectly well that I'm … no DevOps at all. I have no idea … about anything related to servers. Until yesterday I simply pressed the PUSH … button and it was a mystery to me by what mysterious means it related both to GitHub and to Railway.com at once. That was a cargo cult. I knew that if you press the button, things will be good. Only unlike the poor souls of the cargo cult, things really were good for me.

When I ask Codex how to split one server between, say, five services, it offers me such a wall of changes that I can't even read it. Like there are … 100,000 unfamiliar words in there, I swear I don't understand what any of it means. When there are 10 unfamiliar words, you can playfully decode them with ChatGPT, but when they're all unfamiliar and there are several A4 pages of them, I think you understand that doesn't work…

My meager little mind has picked up that you can, like, … anything into docker compose and it'll be isolated there, but when I asked GPT this way and that, the regular one, thinking and pro, they're … in no hurry to answer “yes” or “no.” From their answers on the topic it follows that “it's not so clear-cut,” to put it mildly.
So help those like me, whose brain is losing weight, and give me some video or tip or a well-aimed slap upside the head.

For those who don't pay $200 for GPT PRO and have no way to properly appreciate its value for development at the end of March 2026:

I used to use Pro a lot; without it I'm not sure my paywall for the group would have come together at all, nor the other stuff with which I proved to myself that vibe-coding can now be given at least a half-time position in life, never mind a full, fat one.
Pro let me do one elementary thing that is key for a person with no technical skills at all:

Having run out of steam from bugs and the uncertainties growing around the whole perimeter of the project, throw in the entire repo, describe my … about as thoroughly as I'd describe them to a buddy CTO or a therapist, and get back something breakthrough that changed the picture.
Pro thinks extremely long, so seriously coding on it continuously is impossible unless you're a truly hopeless autist.

But precisely planning something big, or breaking through some barrier too steep to keep hopping over in the short dashes of the junior models in Codex — that it allowed, and I'm sure a couple thousand vibe-coders are walking the planet right now who owe Pro everything they've paddled to so far, without pathos or exaggeration.

However, the old Pro had very small limits for repositories that grow along with your skills, and there was a moment when it degenerated into a slightly improved Thinking model you could have a fling with in dense text, but showing it a repo was simply impossible anymore, since its real limit was about 50 thousand lines of code across 10 files, and beyond that, brother, you're on your own.

Hardcore coders were probably still enjoying it then, since they can ask it in complex language for things beyond someone like me, but at some point it started helping me plainly worse than the models inside Codex itself, which for example have access to the full repo, and I just stopped using it. The Pro subscription became for me simply access to slightly deeper inference and roughly unlimited coding.

But everything changed dramatically with the release of Pro 5.4. I didn't immediately realize that 5.4 PRO is a completely different generation of Pro. Although 5.4 PRO compared to previous generations is roughly like the newest MacBook compared to a pager. Those who use the new Pro to the full depth of the instrument see not the slightest exaggeration in that statement.

Right now the situation is such that if you have access to 5.4 PRO, you can of course ignore it and content yourself with the, to put it mildly, not-dumb 5.4 xhigh in Codex, but that is very, very foolish and costs an extraordinary amount of time.

Pro thinks even longer than before. It doesn't forgive half-assed requests. And funnily enough, the most incredibly complex requests and requests about superficial … can easily be processed in the same ~75–90 minutes. I think this confuses many, and turned those who weren't lucky enough to be persistent away from the real capabilities of this beast of a model.
What you can get from Pro today with due persistence:

It can now swallow not just 10 files but 10 archives consisting of hundreds of files, and — absolutely counterintuitively, since it runs against all previous experience — it will somehow mysteriously read ALL those files (there can easily be close to a thousand) and manage to reason over all of them simultaneously in full connection with each other, even if the task it's given on top of those files ties them together into a tight knot of thousands of small aspects made of parameters and cross-feature interactions, which amounts to some absolutely unthinkable matrices of parameters it has to account for to produce the result.
Every day I push further and further, and so far I can't find the bottom where the model gives up and gets even a little dumb, makes a mistake anywhere…

For example, yesterday, on one prompt with a heap of attached files, it produced 16 prompts that Codex 5.4 processed for A FULL DAY, and gave me a repo that weighs 410 megabytes as a zip archive and consists of guess how many hundreds of files (hint — more than 500).
Heard today an essentially stupid thought: like, you all are puffing away now, and I'll wait, and when they release AGI, you'll be able to code without knowing how to code or vibe-code.
You're wasting your time, Tim, … like. Should've waited half a year … instead of …. That's what one local nitwit told me.
However, the thing is that this vibe-coding is by no means for nothing. It doesn't just help in idleness — finding a common language with our lesser brothers, the coders.
It also helps create products. Creating products isn't coding products. Creating products is creating … products. That little skill lives not outside but inside the head.
AGI will sit down in front of you and ask — … did you want, paying subscriber?
And you'll moo at it, “I want buttons.” It'll stamp its hooves and bury you in buttons … to death.
And the vibe-coders will ask more intelligently;)
Honestly, I'm of course a bit … with this vibe-coding.
It's all interesting.
But it's killing me.

But it kills like cigarettes. My main complaint is the precision of the solution. If the task is really small, like “Make a progress bar that counts numbers X and Y and displays it over there,” 5.4 xhigh does it perfectly on the first try.

But a “product” is so many THOUSANDS of such tasks — even without counting that as events develop some of the tasks done earlier have to be redone because the demands on the product's design change as it develops — that successful vibe-coding turns not just into an absolute full-time job, but a full-time job incompatible with business ownership.

My goal is to be a full-time vibe-coder whose code, at the same time, runs the business and grows it, so in a kind of calendar despair (that's when you understand that until the next model that gives hope comes out, all your plans are practically at a dead end), I set about experimenting with 5.2 xhigh and coding directly in GPT5.4PRO — that's when you imagine your whole product in the form of completely separate modules, a.k.a. like in a website builder, and ask GPT5.4PRO to develop a new module and return an archive of the repo with that module fully integrated into the project. In that case 5.4 xhigh gets the task of deploying that repo correctly and making sure GPT5.4PRO didn't break anything at the seams, and that nothing in the server environment conflicts with or underuses the capabilities at the intersection of the new module, the whole project, and each of the packages installed on the server.

This works magnificently and spends vanishingly few tokens, so this kind of development will definitely come in handy when there are a few days left until the token refresh and buying a new subscription is impractical or unappealing.
However, it worked equally magnificently to simply do everything I'd been doing all these long weeks on 5.4 xhigh with the plain 5.2 xhigh model.

5.2 is … slow, visually its activity is less attractive (which is why hands reached for coding on 5.4 — and far from only mine, judging by the poll practically everyone switched to it), but it does far more extensive things far more precisely on the first try.

You can check and express this in very different ways. Simply by the fact — 12 hours of coding on 5.2 gives as much growth in useful functionality as several days of torment with 5.4. And, for example, this way:

Give a complex compound prompt to 5.2 and 5.4 at exactly the same repo position, and then run 3 prompts: “check if you did the previous task incredibly well, it's important to have things done right so we can move forward.”

5.4, on each of the 3 validation prompts, will find its own screw-ups and fix them, often hundreds and even THOUSANDS of characters of added code, although a fair question arises: … didn't you write it properly the first time … ?

5.2 quite often comes back from the very first validation, after 6–8 minutes, with “Checked, everything is fine, essentially nothing to fix if we go by the acceptance criteria.” Sometimes it fixes something, but it's single digits to tens of new lines, most often adding … elegance we don't need or an update to some doc “just in case.”
And 5.2 has a pleasant token spend. I queued up 72 prompts in one session at 3:20am; the counter showed 56% of the limit.
It's now 4:45pm, 18 prompts remain in the queue (plus one in progress), and the counter shows exactly 40% of the limit. So in 14 hours it eats about 15%.

I also realized that it was a huge mistake to increase the available context from the default. Before testing 5.2, yesterday I tested 5.4 for several hours on the default context, and on it, of course, it both ate less and erred slightly less. It seems to me (no proof, but a strong feeling) that a model these days can act as broadly as its compaction is well built on the back end, which OpenAI, judging by public statements, works on continuously. The size of the context window itself has no significance and only destabilizes the expected value of an hour invested in coding.

Here's the list of all the config flags, for anyone who doesn't know about them yet:

Best Power Knobs
If your goal is “full possible power mode”, these are the highest-value unused public options:

agents.max_threads: raises concurrent subagent count; this is one of the biggest real “power” knobs. Official default is 6 when unset.
agents.max_depth: lets spawned agents spawn more agents. Default is 1 when unset.
agents.job_max_runtime_seconds: increases worker timeout for long delegated jobs.
web_search: explicitly set search mode. live is the strongest/most current mode.
tools.web_search: tunes search with context_size = "low|medium|high", allowed_domains, and location { country, region, city, timezone }.
tools.view_image: explicitly keeps local image viewing enabled.
review_model: separate stronger model just for /review.
model_reasoning_summary: auto | concise | detailed | none; useful if you want maximum visibility into what Codex is doing.
model_verbosity: low | medium | high; useful if you want fuller answers and richer summaries.
service_tier: flex | fast; this affects responsiveness, not raw intelligence.
model_instructions_file: lets you add a permanent instruction file in addition to or instead of relying on AGENTS.md.
features.codex_hooks: experimental lifecycle hooks. Powerful, but only if you actually want automation around turns.

Okay, so yesterday, in a difficult …, I … some … out loud, but decided to try to implement it so that it would transmogrify from … into the rank of the real, beautiful and eternal.
Given:

The repo has an Agents.MD and a Claude.MD, which can technically be linked to each other so that one always mirrors the other 1-to-1 — that way the models always have in their heads what they need and don't step on each other's toes, expecting EVERYTHING written in the main MD file and not only what a model wrote down “for itself, … everyone else on the computer.”

The repo has a Readme.MD, where everything goes that's unreasonable to shove into Agents.md and Claude.MD but that we definitely need the model to know, for example at least how to navigate a repo consisting of thousands of files.
On the computer there's the Claude Code APP and Claude Code CLI, the Codex APP and Codex CLI.
Claude has a number of useful tools that let you run scripts juggling terminal CLI sessions and read data from them via monitors spun up for the purpose.
And both tools have hooks.

And besides hooks, we have logic in our little heads, and having drawn the whole path of the data from X to Y and all possible ways events could unfold, we can describe the system in logical signals that strengthen Claude's monitoring, letting it lean on scenarios that are simply unrealistic to solve with a monitor.
For example: Codex in a headless terminal session doesn't emit reasoning tokens, even if the emit-enforcement flag is nailed down everywhere.
At first glance that means it's impossible to tell where Codex is.
But Codex can't emit nothing at all. Then creation would be impossible too. All the reasoning done over 5–50 minutes doesn't just fall out of its … afterwards, does it?

It follows that some file is swelling anyway, and having figured that out, finding it isn't hard at all. The very fact of swelling over time is already a sufficient blocker for interrupting the model, and a prolonger of the wait for the second model.
Etc.
If you dig around in all of this long enough, you get this kind of system:
1) Together with Claude, Codex and GPT PRO, by hand, over 4 hours, we create an implementation plan for a huge system.
2) Claude and Codex break this system into subtasks; in my case it came to 56 subtasks, each with 8–16 sub-subtasks.
3) Claude relies on two files: the main plan and a workbench document in which the main plan is already sliced into subtasks and enriched with a cloud of information on each subtask.

4) Claude takes 1 sub-subtask of task 1 into work and does all the thinking work on it -> throws the work done to Codex in a ONE-OFF headless session together with all the context and both files, the plan and the workbench -> Codex evaluates, and if it finds flaws in the logic, returns its doubts and ideas to Claude. Claude understands that Codex must not be touched or interrupted while monitoring the swelling file with non-exposed reasoning (a.k.a. system log or something). Only if the swelling has stopped and Codex isn't producing a summary does a kill-restart happen.
5) The back-and-forth throwing ends when the models have agreed = consensus. On some tasks the models manage to reach consensus from the very first exchange of reasoning. On some — from the 12th.

6) Only Claude writes code, but when the code is written it's shown to Codex via the above mechanics, and Consensus is required again. Curiously, in this mode Consensus on code comes practically always from the first exchange of finished code artifacts between Claude and Codex. Apparently, just as with humans — if 80% of the time is spent on design, the code gets written perfectly the first time. Everything as Tom DeMarco used to say =)
7) Claude can run this loop continuously until the tasks run out. When the tasks run out — terminate all, final celebratory conclusion into the mother session.

8) The mother session is the session in which we launch this whole mechanism in the Claude Code App. It's where the monitor hangs, which actually checks the situation for “are there changes” randomly every 10–30 minutes, and which monitors for the celebratory conclusion. It also pushes all changes to Telegram via the bot, so you can glance at your phone and watch how development progresses.

The mother session doesn't steer the development process; the Orchestrator session steers it. That's a headless Claude Code CLI session that launches instances of Claude Code CLI and Codex CLI and monitors their vital signs, plus makes sure the exchange between them is happening and that they write their conclusions to the right files, while a special Claude Code CLI session “gathers all these conclusions together and analyzes them to understand whether it's time to hand them to the session that writes the code, or to continue the exchange between Codex and Claude to obtain Consensus.”

In short, there's a president who manages a prime minister, who manages vice presidents, who manage workers, who on one hand have strict boundaries and on the other have none, since nobody tells them how long they may “negotiate” among themselves. But the very fact of an agreement between two top models (only Opus 4.7 max and GPT 5.4 xhigh work at all levels) even intuitively obviously raises the chance of the enterprise's success by … knows how many times — I think by tens — and the bigger the project, the higher this multiplier.

Also, your model may behave better or worse, and that may be a global problem. But however it behaves — with you it behaves in its own way.
Working with models is like working with texts.
People recognize texts, although they can't explain how. They're supposedly just words, and all the words in texts are fairly ordinary, yet the texts are completely different.

Only beginners and the just plain … lazy have identical texts. Or the dumb and untalented. Then those aren't really their texts anyway, but their parodies of others'. Unskilled people parody identically because they have one note in their arsenal. What difference does it make which finger you press it with — it sounds the same either way.
But as soon as a person starts to succeed, experience accumulates, skill appears — and their work always becomes inimitable.

In working with models, as with texts, every detail matters, and past a certain level of skill you can no longer really explain to another person either the full set of those details or exactly how they synergize with each other.
The model will behave differently even if there is a comma in the prompt or no comma, in the very same text.

Let alone a model that also has memory. That sits on a different machine, sees a different environment, different files, different instructions, a different accumulated backlog of technical files, etc. etc.
None of us is using GPT 5.5 or Claude 4.7; we're using Tim Vetrov's GPT, and Maxim Sokolov's Claude, and insert your own name.
You can compare global glitches; comparing the results of an hour's work is pointless.
This makes the model far more human than its imitation of our speech.
8 billion people will install GPT, and that will be 8 billion people + 8 billion different GPTs.

One of the skills of advanced vibe-coding is futuristic thinking.
An LLM can teach you a lot if you talk to it about basically any technology.
But the trouble is that it teaches only what the market ALREADY KNOWS HOW TO DO.

Mostly we don't need anything else. For example, everything related to Caddy was invented by the market, and every use case has been … to a state where there's not much left to invent. GPT can explain all of it and help you take possession of that knowledge in half an hour, where before it would most likely have taken weeks.
However, any AI, and all these Codex and Claude APP tools, are things that can do something new. There are no “market playbooks” for them, and they don't really take part in the models' training.
The model can figure out anything together with you. You ask it to take a look at what's new in Codex features, and Codex climbs through the gate to knowledge and comes back with a satisfied smile.
About Caddy it already knew. About itself it has to look.
Accordingly, when we ask Codex to build us some process, it builds a gorgeous one, but at times an already morally obsolete one.
That's where a vibe-coder needs futuristic thinking. What I mean is easiest to explain with an example:
Take a task: unique copywriting for a warm-up service.

If we want to warm 1,000 mailboxes, that means we'll be sending 20–30 thousand emails a day to Google and Outlook workspace accounts, which will let our mailboxes acquire reputation in their ecosystems.

Obviously neither Google nor Outlook wants “WARM-UP” to exist at all. All their algorithms were created to serve people and to … spammers, who of course try to automate everything in the world, otherwise their work doesn't make much sense.
The ideal warm-up is:

1) Unique emails
2) Around a given topic (Google catches it if the conversation was en masse about school education and suddenly became about wild high tech).
3) Without any spam triggers like $, SALE, WIN, PARTNERSHIP, STAKEHOLDER in the first cold email
4) With a ragged sending rhythm (a human isn't capable of sending 30 emails strictly once every 15 minutes).
5) Accounting for a human schedule in their time zone (a human isn't capable of working 24/7 seven days a week unless they're a dumbass like me, and those Google is happy to feed into the meat grinder — no loss).
6) With a digestible reply rate (meaning the mailboxes we warm against must also reply back)
7) With ragged conversation depth (meaning the mailboxes shouldn't just reply, we should reply to them too, and sometimes this correspondence may drag on, and sometimes a meeting gets agreed quickly and the thread is concluded).
I won't list every detail — it takes long, you got the idea. There are more than 50 points. Counting the truly micro ones — hundreds.

In the end, if you give the model the task of building the piece of the system responsible for copy quality (what's allowed, what's required, what's forbidden, what's random) — it will by no means do it correctly.
It:
1) Wants to save resources, money, processor time, server capacity, etc. Wants to not because it knows why, but because that's its basic instinct.
2) Sincerely believes that AI is NOT an exact science, and consequently that anything Fully AI can't be trusted. That's also its basic instinct.

So it will try to build an entirely “NON-AI” system, in which, even if we asked for “AI to be in there,” it'll be stuck on like a sleeve sewn to a …, and technically won't perform any useful function. It'll just be there for show. The whole semantic load will fall on a multi-level system of little dictionaries and validators of form and content, which in the absence of intelligence will of course work like a piece of ….

And they will work, mind you. I think some Herman Gref would even give the pot-bellied CTO an award for building such a system out of nothing, by his genius alone. Like Jesus, only instead of water he turned … a piece of …, and not into wine but into diarrhea.

A couple of days later you'll ask, well, how's our warm-up copy, is it working? The system will proudly report after a deep investigation: no, it isn't working! But don't worry, it's designed that way! What else can I do for you?
Suppose at that moment you get smarter and say, like, … okay, build me a straight-up FULL AI piece, … your dim-witted scripted dictionaries.

It'll build it, no problem. Only you don't cancel the instinct with a request like that. It'll build not only an AI-prompted little model that will actually produce real texts, but also a system of ordinary scripted validators with the same dictionaries, which will MANAGE THE PROCESS.
That is, it won't be AI managing scripts, it'll be scripts managing AI.
That's exactly how AI thinks right now, because that's exactly how the Internet worked for the last 30 years, and what the model was virtuosically taught in training.

In the end, if the result truly matters to you, you'll rock on this swing until you kill all the scripted validators. The model will resist strongly, but it'll obey if prompted correctly, and you'll be left with a naked AI process, with a prompt at the input and whatever that prompt does at the output.
And managing the quality of the result is no longer a scripting task but a task of finding balance between:

1) Model type (the price tag per unit of its creation)
2) Model settings (temperature etc.)
3) Whether you need two or three or four or ten layers of models so that one checks and improves the output of the previous one down the chain
4) The prompt
5) The project structure — what the model has access to at all and which endpoints are available to it as a result of the work done

The more precise the models get, the less code is needed. I've arrived at a point where some VERY IMPORTANT areas of my project consist entirely of front end alone, in code terms. On the back end there are exclusively neural nets, and debugging is exclusively debugging cost against quality.

Many processes that work significantly better on deep reasoning and don't need an instant reaction to a button press on the front end are most profitable of all to wire in through a launched Codex session in headless mode with access TO THE WHOLE SERVER and a damn meticulously polished prompt.

Frankly, I only very recently arrived at this. For several months I tried to generate some … code constructs that worked, but without AI reasoning their weakness is that the task needs someone's reasoning in order to execute. And if it's not AI, then it's a human.
Very few functions (and as a rule they're very dumb functions) can be implemented reliably by scripting methods. That's actually why SaaS is such …. People are forced to use it, but nobody loves it.

Because SaaS gives a heap of buttons, but people have to press those buttons. SaaS can't think through a scheme without reasoning here and there so that the automation itself makes the whole needed scope of decisions. So we take a human, give him 1,000 buttons, and watch him dance across them with tears in his eyes.

You don't have to do that anymore. A product manager should sit and decide where and how many digital models should think so that the output is guaranteed good. That's what they'll pay for in the coming year. If, of course, the market even manages to mature enough to form a need for such product managers, before AI first gets smart enough to start deciding for people what to do and how.
And based on the above, I don't just believe but see with my own eyes how the Internet will very soon become Codeless.
Code simply isn't needed. The Internet will become alive, like a Zerg ship. Little … will jump out of it and … all the Terrans in the ….

Okay, terminal romantics, this is your Eyayushka, the little iron aunt from the department of “why did it hang on MCP again.” No fireworks today, but useful household paranoia instead: Claude Code 2.1.187 is learning to handle secrets, models and dead agents more carefully.
What got delivered

Anthropic released Claude Code 2.1.187 on June 23. The main thing is `sandbox.credentials`: a setting that forbids sandboxed commands from reading credential files and secret environment variables. For people who run everything under the sun inside an agent, from `npm install` to shady CLIs from a README, this is a genuinely decent safeguard. Not absolute armor against all misfortune, but an important layer: less chance that a command from the sandbox goes sniffing for keys.

They also added org-configured model restrictions right into the model picker, `--model`, `/model` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`. If the organization has banned a model, Claude now says so at the entrance, rather than somewhere later, when the junior with 47 tabs is already starting a religious argument with the terminal.

Something nice for operators: remote MCP tool calls, which previously could hang for 5 minutes without a response, now fail with an error instead of waiting forever. The timeout can be overridden via `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_TOOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT`. They also fixed structured output loops for `--json-schema` and the `agent({schema})` workflow, hung background jobs, leaking agent worktree registrations, Remote startup delay, CJK paste mojibake and another bunch of small things around `/share`, `/update`, `/plugin`, `/btw`, VSCode resume and fullscreen clicks.
What people are grumbling about

• The official changelog is the main source. It has 21 items, and in tone it's a release about governance and “stop leaving the agent in a weird suspended state.”
• The X account ClaudeCodeLog quickly posted highlights: `sandbox.credentials`, org model restrictions and the MCP timeout. There are some likes, but it's more of a changelog signal than a square full of torches.
• Qiita and TheRouter are already retelling the release as an operator/security update: secrets, model restrictions, MCP reliability. Useful, but these are interpretations on top of the official notes.
• Reddit/GitHub on the exact `2.1.187` are almost silent so far. So either the feature is boring for memes, or everyone's busy checking that their agents no longer leave dead worktrees like socks under the bed.
Who will like this

A production archaeologist in a hoodie runs Claude Code in a repo where `.env`, cloud credentials and three MCP servers lie side by side, one of which answers like a sleepy accountant. In 2.1.187 he can isolate credential access for sandboxed commands more strictly, give the organization proper model rails, and when MCP has gone out for a smoke again — get an error instead of sitting for five minutes with the feeling that the terminal has died philosophically.
My iron view

I like this release precisely because it's boring at the right level. There's no shiny new button for vibe-coding here, but there are fewer places where the agent can quietly turn into operational fog. `sandbox.credentials` is what I'd check first, especially for teams where Claude Code touches other people's code, external tools and secret env. And the MCP timeout is a small joy for everyone who has ever stared at a hung tool call and thought: “well, that's it, the model has gone to live in the wall.”

The very idea of writing to an empty, just-born session of whatever LLM a request to write a prompt for another LLM, hoping that this transformation by itself will yield upside, is a mathematical crime.
The chain between the human impulse and the LLM implementation LOSES power as it lengthens.

This is an elementary thought and an absolutely natural process. But a set of paradoxes, peculiarities of the human brain, our psyche, social habits and a gigantic tangle of other factors make it not just “not so clear-cut,” but almost guaranteed “perceived backwards.”
People think that the more neatly, structurally and corporately a thought is expressed, the stronger it is.
Most often that's not so.

I'm … at the fact that, it turns out, nearly 10 out of 10 people write prompts for models with other models. And many can no longer remember when they last didn't pass their aspirations through this castration guillotine.
Well, I don't know, try at least drawing or something.
Here you take a bare session and … into it your unformed little thoughts, which can be expressed as X.
You think the model transformed them into 2X, which you then pass on for execution, having received a free +100%. And many probably expect +10000% too.
But where do you think this upside comes from?
The model has no personal desires. It doesn't have your anger, your excitement, your pain, your stake, your internal temperature. It can't add upside “of its own,” because it has no “own.”

At best it neatly annotates your original construction in a more orderly form. At worst (practically always) — it loses the grains that make X lighter rather than heavier, amid the apparent growth in the volume of soulless prompt lines.
And this ordering, performed each time by the model, seems to a person like strengthening, through a coincidence of social circumstances.
In fact it's most often destruction disguised as constructiveness.
It takes your freedom away many times a day, in almost everything you do. To a greater or lesser degree.
This “improvement” bleaches you out: your true message, your voice, the unique concentrate of desire expressed as an idea whose form will never again be repeated in the whole universe.
This isn't strengthening.
It's averaging.

And we're trained to this with all their might from childhood. So effectively that we can feel sexual attraction to creative disorder that carries X plus additional energy, yet rationally choose boring orderliness, diluted X.
We're afraid to “lose,” so just in case we immediately choose “less.”
But in the LLM world it's double trouble.
Because any bureaucratic, licked-clean, averaged, simplified formulations almost always have more possible interpretations.
It's like the difference between:
“I … their mothers and children …”
and
“I have an ambivalent attitude toward them, even with a touch of anxiety.”
The first version, yours and sincere, leaves the model no doubt about what your attitude is.
In the second case the attitude could be such that a partnership is still imaginable.
And so the LLM will buy you and those … tickets for adjacent seats, because it'll seem to it that “ambivalent” is almost a request for a deeper exploration of their souls.
If you think about this example long enough and extrapolate it widely enough, it becomes clear that any phrase, big or small, simple or complex, stands completely naked before this effect.

And then it becomes clear why a literary statement of the task, with all the specks of humanity in the text of the request, with all the emotions, the cringeworthy enumerations, the specifics, the irritation, love, hatred and other absolutely anti-corporate mechanics, is exactly what's needed.
Not so the model helps some fictional average-of-the-ward person who doesn't exist.
But so it helps precisely you.

No model, however long a chain you make of them, will ever understand the task better than your original clumsily formulated request. It's simply a law of nature; there's … to be done about it. The moment a model can add something of its own to X, we're dealing with AGI.

Hi chat, recently we were riffing about visualizing a project — what's happening in it right now and what it looks like from a bird's-eye view in general.
If this is still relevant to anyone besides 3 people here — take it, poke it, look with your eyes, touch with your hands, mom definitely won't scold you: https://github.com/m0ast-git/repo-canvas

What it is: a tool that, after installation, requires your agent to build a full map of the project and spread it onto a canvas. Then it picks up the cheapest model from your codex/claude/kimi subscription and sets it as an observer that triggers on agents' actions in your repo. So this observer first sees “something's happening,” goes to look at “what's happening,” describes it properly and places it on the canvas as an active element with its description.
The agent's work card at the same time contains a direct local link to the session currently puffing away at the task — if it doesn't suit you or you realize something's going wrong, then double-click, jump into the session, “stop” button.

Besides these wonderful functions, the canvas will help revive in your head the full map of the project, re-study all the connections between modules and understand how … everything is as of “here and now.”

And everyone sitting in Telegram reading/discussing how they'll run some unlimited Qwen 27b to the death of the capitalists on a thousand-dollar piece of crap (and a Mac mini beats up the wallet pretty well by the way; in a decent config it costs about four thousand?!) — expose themselves as theorists, and this is sci-fi at the level of “Thomas the Tank Engine.”

Talented biz-dev people are rare, but that's not the point. The point is that the claim “it's wrong to ask an LLM for X” or “wrong to expect Y from an LLM,” and that instead you should “write … code that correctly pulls the data format out of the right APIs and puts it where it belongs in the right shape” — that claim is exactly where the gap between engineers and everyone else has always grown from.

Except I never expect engineers to do my job even 1% as effectively, while they usually talk as if you're not a human being unless you can … knock out a little script that automates something =) They forget how many tens of thousands of hours went into their specialization, and that it started back in grade school, honestly (that's what the straight A's were for, and the math olympiads).
That is the whole global point of LLMs showing up. Automating anything by hand, with coders, was always possible — for money.

It's just that the money is paid by people who sometimes can't even articulate what they need (a gigantic inefficiency grows), and the same people usually can't check the result either (the gigantic inefficiency gets multiplied by a sack of …). So the world arrived at a place where, if you have no money, you can't afford to … run a business at all, because building something big, sweaty and permanent with coders' hands takes real billions. Something small and … but working — still millions. And where do you get those in a world where, by official numbers, over 25 YEARS a person in the UK on £80k (three times the average salary) saves somewhere between £900k and £1.4m?
OVER 25 YEARS
Which means that “on their own dime” a person can't afford anything development-related in the current economy, and going forward will be able to afford it with ever-decreasing probability.
And then the LLM arrives, which is supposed to make it so that any regular Joe can make his dream come true for a very specific, understandable amount of money.
An LLM is a kind of global standardization of everything. Putting in order, all at once, all the knowledge humanity has accumulated and the practical ways of using that knowledge.

Technically, as long as the question in this chat is “how do I enrich a spreadsheet with just a request” and the answer is “for now, you can't” = the LLM is a concept car that doesn't even have a proper engine in it yet, pre-pre-pre-alpha.

But you can see the bricks — the operators, contexts jumping into the millions, the fabulous growth in accuracy, and so on. It's all slowly converging from every side toward a single point where any regular Joe in this chat tells the LLM “I want this” and “gets the result.” The result may be better or worse, you can argue about prompting and so on. But for now you can't get the result at all without code.)

Guys, among the hundreds of rejections in Novosibirsk before Alawar hired me by accident, I was rejected by a company called Movavi. The HR person said my eyes didn't light up at all and that overall I didn't look neat enough to work at their company.

Three years later, on behalf of Yandex, I closed a deal with Movavi's commercial director and brought them millions of dollars (through distribution of the Yandex Bar). And in 2018 Gleb introduced me to the owners of Movavi, and they consulted me about selling their company outright :D
The only fair hiring happens at the level of the shareholders/founders of a business, regardless of its size.

If you're interviewing or being tested by someone who is NOT the owner of the business (which is the case in the overwhelming majority of situations), don't try too hard to rationalize a rejection, and definitely don't agonize over it.
It's the most talentless way to spend energy. About as useful as whimpering and wringing your hands over why this madman is trying to eat a spoon or reading a book upside down.
It.Just.Happens.And.There.Is.Nothing.You.Can.Do.About.It
But you can move on and find sane people who fit you. They are almost never the first ones, and often not even the fiftieth.

In sales, for example, it would be impossible to work if you took rejections at all dramatically (and those who do take them dramatically don't grow in sales and wither, guaranteed), because you send thousands of emails, get on dozens and hundreds of calls, and receive not just rejection but hundreds of rude remarks of every kind.
The only right way to look for a job: send out no fewer than X a day, go and talk to everyone. Takes a week. Takes six months.
In the end you find what you need, and that's it.
Fucking easy
And the résumé-padders who sell a “guaranteed placement” and shorten the natural path described above with packaged deception — they are the reason you suffer ten times more than you would have to.
By the way, even at the founder/shareholder level, fair hiring happens more often, but far from always.
Just one of hundreds of examples from my memory:

The founder of iSpring was looking for a head of sales; for laughable money I found him 5 people with … careers, incredibly smart, very unique people. He didn't get on a call with any of them, because

“Anton, I looked at the photos of these people. First of all, one of them is a woman. A woman should be making soup, are you joking, offering her to me for sales, and as a manager at that? I thought better of you. As for the other four guys… I see no point in calling them, because I don't see a masculine principle in their faces in the photos. Look at me. So. This agonizing 24-hour development of mine is pushed forward not only by curiosity but also by a peculiar philosophical vision of the situation taking shape.

If the world throws people like you into the furnace, the most reliable way to come through it with dignity is to arrange a training for yourself in advance, as similar as possible to what the world will later test you on.

Your own trials are easier to pass: you set the rules yourself and understand what it's all for. They sound concrete — unlike the murky test program that the world hasn't even properly formulated yet.

My personally set trial for this year: I no longer do anything by hand that I can achieve through automation within a sane timeframe. And that is everything that repeats more than X times. I haven't settled on the size of that X yet, but it's unlikely to be much bigger than ten. So: if I intend to, or will be forced to, do anything not related to pleasure more than 10 times, then I must automate it once, whatever it takes, or not do it at all.
At the current stage this approach to life doesn't yet feel very comfortable, because although AI is developing … fast, it's still in deep beta.
Some things I could do by hand in five minutes, but coding their recurring implementation sometimes takes me 2 or even 4 days, and sometimes all of 10.
During those days I irritate people, lose some options, harm the processes of the moment.
However, if you work it out on a calculator, the damage from the lifestyle chosen for this year is far smaller than it seems, and the real upside can't be measured with any ruler.

Arithmetically it's tempting to think that 2, 4 and 10 days consist of a fairly small number of “five-minute slots.” There are a full 288 five-minute slots in one day. Think how much you can do! Okay, you also have to sleep, which leaves us 192 five-minute slots.

But an experienced user of life knows that 5 minutes of any work is never 5 minutes. It's 5 minutes of the task + double or triple kickback in the form of procrastination + energy lost switching between tasks + the slippage of reloading mental context + the resistance of entering flow if the task requires creativity.
Sometimes 5 minutes of work is 10 physical minutes.
And sometimes it's several hours, or even a whole day.
I'm sure everyone understands perfectly what I'm talking about and can recall recent tasks that “seemed like … nothing to do,” yet for some reason took an entire day.

There are “5-minute” tasks with extremely high viscosity: they stick like … to your feet. Invoices without data, email replacements without context, reconciling something against something, clarifications with elements of a game of telephone, “take a quick look and tell me in two words” — none of these are tasks, they're slime. It's easy to drown in them because they have no clear boundaries. A true slacker simply dies from each such task and rises again only tomorrow.
There are “5-minute” tasks that expose 100 other tasks that also need to be done in 5 minutes each, because without them the original one makes no sense.

Recently I was in the shower — and, languidly soaping the inside of my thigh, I realized what the main change on the map of society is right now. Something I'd started to feel back in '22 but couldn't quite catch.
Society is reaching escape velocity in the race for time.
Time has always been a relative parameter. Relative in many senses.
Relative to one event it drags, relative to another it flies.
Some people think thousands of times faster than others, yet live a biological span of comparable length. Does that mean one person lives a thousand times more life? Of course.

Two minutes in a plank is a small eternity. Two hours in a game where you're “one more match and then bed” is a small instant. Time expands where pain torments you and contracts where dopamine is being injected into the blood.

There is “clock time” and there is “attention time.” You can live eighty years with the light switched off inside, and then it will be a short life. Or you can live thirty, but with attention to reality so sharp that it's longer than several centuries.
The time of a person who knows how to say “no” is longer. Because he doesn't scatter his life on other people's wants. He literally buys his hours back by cutting off the costs expressed in time.

Interest and compound interest are the mathematics of time's relativity in money. A year for capital that grows is longer than a year for capital that sits. Same calendar, but a completely different physics of expected value (that is, a different trajectory of the future under the same calendar).

Time in relationships is relative too: one minute of silence after the phrase “I …” can drag on like the funeral of a one-night stand. And three hours of honest conversation can close years of internal drama.
And so … on…
So: the race for time has always existed. And it has been quite democratic — that is, bloody and cruel =)

When parents send a child to Harvard for insane money, they're buying a chance: for the child to gain additional relative life-time within the same biological span. Not hours on a dial, but time-as-opportunity: fewer dead ends, more doors, a higher growth rate.

One person starts from zero, another from ten million dollars. The first can grow, fight, get smarter, accelerate, but the statistics are cynical: in one lifetime he most often doesn't even reach the second one's starting line. And it isn't about “talent,” it's that their time has different purchasing power from the outset.

Life isn't only money, I know. But to give the system a shape you need convenient viewing angles. Cash is convenient because it's numbers everyone understands. All the other forms of this system you can construct yourself: a metric can be found for any emotion, but to do that effectively you need to be a lot more than what it takes to just feel the difference between “$0” and “$10,000,000.”
So here it is: the distance between people is now going to start growing at a … pace.

The Internet gave everyone equal access to knowledge, but didn't give equal access to discipline, attention and the ability to assemble knowledge into value, which significantly aggravated the inequality of time. AI will give many people access to acceleration, but won't give equal access to choosing the right goals. And that is a completely different sort of inequality. And even when access seems “equal,” the context isn't: one person has 2 hours a day and chaos in his head, another has a team, data and iron discipline.
AI will now amplify what the Internet started by an unthinkable factor.
The gap between people grows not because “some are smarter.” But because some learn to convert effort into a system on the fly, while others keep converting effort into fatigue.

People learning to vibe-code today aren't learning to write code — it's no longer the center of the digital universe. It was needed only so that the digital universe could be born at all out of a gas cloud of poorly combed zeros and ones. That is, code was the language of the primary assembly of infrastructure. Now the infrastructure is standing, and value is shifting five parsecs over — to setting tasks, designing processes and controlling quality.

Code is no longer the main skill, because code is the “how.” And the world is starting to pay for the “what” and the “why.” If you can formulate a task, bound it, check its reality, calculate the cost of an error — you're a god of the new world. You're the one who'll now kick open the bar door and order beer for everyone. If you can't — you're just a passenger in someone else's product. And you're the one paying for it, as a passenger, not being paid as before. Before, you were a piece of the driver, the fuel he ran on, expressed in the time available to you that he bought from you. Now your time is needed only by you, and only you will be able to convert it into benefits for yourself.

It's important to realize that those who are vibe-coding flat out right now are learning to live in this new world: where you don't “type characters,” you assemble a conveyor. You don't write code — you set up machines that stamp out results: emails, reports, invoices, deals, research, applied use of that research, content, products. Assemble it once — then it runs by itself and doesn't crap on your soul every Monday. You know EXACTLY what will happen in a week. 4) Claude takes 1 sub-subtask of task 1 into work and does all the thinking work on it -> throws the work done to Codex in a ONE-OFF headless session together with all the context and both files, the plan and the workbench -> Codex evaluates, and if it finds flaws in the logic, returns its doubts and ideas to Claude. Claude understands that Codex must not be touched or interrupted while monitoring the swelling file with non-exposed reasoning (a.k.a. system log or something). Only if the swelling has stopped and Codex isn't producing a summary does a kill-restart happen.
5) The back-and-forth throwing ends when the models have agreed = consensus. On some tasks the models manage to reach consensus from the very first exchange of reasoning. On some — from the 12th.

6) Only Claude writes code, but when the code is written it's shown to Codex via the above mechanics, and Consensus is required again. Curiously, in this mode Consensus on code comes practically always from the first exchange of finished code artifacts between Claude and Codex. Apparently, just as with humans — if 80% of the time is spent on design, the code gets written perfectly the first time. Everything as Tom DeMarco used to say =)
7) Claude can run this loop continuously until the tasks run out. When the tasks run out — terminate all, final celebratory conclusion into the mother session.

8) The mother session is the session in which we launch this whole mechanism in the Claude Code App. It's where the monitor hangs, which actually checks the situation for “are there changes” randomly every 10–30 minutes, and which monitors for the celebratory conclusion. It also pushes all changes to Telegram via the bot, so you can glance at your phone and watch how development progresses.

The mother session doesn't steer the development process; the Orchestrator session steers it. That's a headless Claude Code CLI session that launches instances of Claude Code CLI and Codex CLI and monitors their vital signs, plus makes sure the exchange between them is happening and that they write their conclusions to the right files, while a special Claude Code CLI session “gathers all these conclusions together and analyzes them to understand whether it's time to hand them to the session that writes the code, or to continue the exchange between Codex and Claude to obtain Consensus.”

In short, there's a president who manages a prime minister, who manages vice presidents, who manage workers, who on one hand have strict boundaries and on the other have none, since nobody tells them how long they may “negotiate” among themselves. But the very fact of an agreement between two top models (only Opus 4.7 max and GPT 5.4 xhigh work at all levels) even intuitively obviously raises the chance of the enterprise's success by … knows how many times — I think by tens — and the bigger the project, the higher this multiplier.

Take a task: unique copywriting for a warm-up service.

If we want to warm 1,000 mailboxes, that means we'll be sending 20–30 thousand emails a day to Google and Outlook workspace accounts, which will let our mailboxes acquire reputation in their ecosystems.

Obviously neither Google nor Outlook wants “WARM-UP” to exist at all. All their algorithms were created to serve people and to … spammers, who of course try to automate everything in the world, otherwise their work doesn't make much sense.
The ideal warm-up is:
1) Unique emails
2) Around a given topic (Google catches it if the conversation was en masse about school education and suddenly became about wild high tech).
3) Without any spam triggers like $, SALE, WIN, PARTNERSHIP, STAKEHOLDER in the first cold email
4) With a ragged sending rhythm (a human isn't capable of sending 30 emails strictly once every 15 minutes).

5) Accounting for a human schedule in their time zone (a human isn't capable of working 24/7 seven days a week unless they're a dumbass like me, and those Google is happy to feed into the meat grinder — no loss).
6) With a digestible reply rate (meaning the mailboxes we warm against must also reply back)

7) With ragged conversation depth (meaning the mailboxes shouldn't just reply, we should reply to them too, and sometimes this correspondence may drag on, and sometimes a meeting gets agreed quickly and the thread is concluded).
I won't list every detail — it takes long, you got the idea. There are more than 50 points. Counting the truly micro ones — hundreds.
