Hi chat, recently we were riffing about visualizing a project — what's happening in it right now and what it looks like from a bird's-eye view in general.
If this is still relevant to anyone besides 3 people here — take it, poke it, look with your eyes, touch with your hands, mom definitely won't scold you: https://github.com/m0ast-git/repo-canvas

What it is: a tool that, after installation, requires your agent to build a full map of the project and spread it onto a canvas. Then it picks up the cheapest model from your codex/claude/kimi subscription and sets it as an observer that triggers on agents' actions in your repo. So this observer first sees “something's happening,” goes to look at “what's happening,” describes it properly and places it on the canvas as an active element with its description.

The agent's work card at the same time contains a direct local link to the session currently puffing away at the task — if it doesn't suit you or you realize something's going wrong, then double-click, jump into the session, “stop” button.

Besides these wonderful functions, the canvas will help revive in your head the full map of the project, re-study all the connections between modules and understand how … everything is as of “here and now.”
Bonus video with a live demo on my project
In short, my setup as of today is this:
2x GPT PRO MAX ($400)

But
GPT is the most throttled in both directions:
1) There's a great deal it's not allowed to do, and believe me, everything it's not allowed affects absolutely everything it does, including what it is allowed.

2) Each next step up in reasoning doesn't just make it smarter but again FORBIDS IT TO BE DUMBER. Hence the manic-ness and the hours/days where it could have coped perfectly in minutes. Hundreds of files where a piece of one would have been enough, etc.

And this looping from point 2 isn't baked into the model, but is a side effect that worsens during work. The deeper into the woods, the fatter these wolves. So any reasoning levels above Medium should be used only to think with, but you can work with them only on a sufficiently narrow/simple task in which the model simply won't have time to go insane and do more harm than good.

In the end it turned out that GPT 5.6 Sol MEDIUM is essentially the same GPT 5.5 xhigh, only smarter thanks to the properties the model has independent of reasoning. For example, 5.6's eyes are set much farther apart than 5.5's, and thanks to that it sees the parts of a task 5.5 doesn't.
In short, I lost all interest in using 5.5 once I figured out 5.6.

Yesterday I wrote a post about the suffering caused by having to take responsibility not only for the code but for the design too. And for me that's a problem. Because when you vibe-code a solution, at first you can set aside existential things like code cleanliness, security, bugs, and orient by the result — does it work or not.

But when it comes to visuals and usability, the nuances begin. The first thing AI gives you for the request “create a website” is a blue-violet gradient, the Inter font and a typical landing-page skeleton.

By the way, this AI slop of websites is the fault of the popular CSS framework Tailwind; back in 2019 they made indigo the default color of buttons in their components, the tutorials spread across all of GitHub, and the models learned that median.

Tailwind's creator Adam Wathan later publicly admitted he chose indigo not for design reasons but as a neutral placeholder for demos. And that shade of lavender has already been nicknamed “VibeCode Purple.”

And then the circulation of AI slop in the nature of web design begins. Vibe-coded sites get onto the web, the next generation of models already learns from them, the average self-reinforces. Plus the agent additionally narrows the choice to what's easier to lay out.
So how do you break this purple circle if you have no designer's eye? Here's what I fed my agent and myself:

— ui-skills.com — a catalog of design-engineering skills for agents. Inside are skills from shadcn, Anthropic, Emil Kowalski and others. Plug in via CLI or MCP, and the agent starts laying out by the rules rather than by its own generic habits
— ui.shadcn.com — the industry standard, the foundation of the design systems of half the modern web. The component code goes right into your project, so agents edit it freely and know this library better than any other. Free
— coss.com/ui — a fresh library of a pile of components on top of Base UI, tuned among other things for AI applications. Open source
— designsystemchecklist.com — a checklist. A list of what must be covered in a design system, from colors to documentation. Feed it to the agent as a quality frame against which it checks your front end
— beautifului.dev — a component library specifically for AI interfaces. Chats, streaming loaders, code blocks, agent-action confirmation cards, workflow visualization. Copy and paste. Free
— beui.dev — animated components for React and Next.js on Framer Motion and Tailwind. Modals, buttons, tabs, toasts, docs. Installs via the shadcn CLI. Base is open source, there's a paid Pro
— rareui.com — a small collection of fun animated React components. Folders, letter gravity, liquid ball. Each component is one file, installed with one command. Completely free
— transitions.dev — a catalog of ready-made transitions and micro-animations. Modal opening, skeletons, number animation, card resizing. Copy the code or plug it into the agent as a separate skill. Base is free, the rest in Pro
— emilkowal.ski/ui/you-dont-need-animations — an essay by Emil Kowalski (author of the sonner and vaul libraries) on when animations hurt. For example, that frequent actions are better not animated and everything should stay faster than 300 ms. Feed it to the agent so it doesn't turn the interface into a cartoon

1) The prompt must describe in the greatest detail the cause-and-effect relationships from your head, in full; you literally have to write a manual, there's no other way. Delegating it to the LLM to write for you won't work. It will shorten and destroy the meaning of the causality, shriveling it to the point where it can't be unfolded back to the quality you need. I … with this for two months.

2) You have to make sure that nowhere within the radius of the model's operations is there a single scripted validator, verifier, gate, etc. There should be no determinism there except a data transport tool, which is passive rather than active. It accepts data from the LLM, which again understands very well how to put it there because it was very well described and explained to it.
3) You have to make sure that in the giant prompt with all the explanations there are no strict prohibitions.
Often people have DON'T, DON'T, DON'T, DON'T in there — that doesn't work.

Cumulative prohibitions usually embrace the task so broadly that the model's goal becomes not to complete the assignment but not to violate the prohibition. That affects quality… well, how to put it… by about 99.5% =))))))))
If the research is really big, it should be not one worker but sequential workers, each performing its own task. In my researcher for client campaigns there are…. 36 such workers in a row

From time to time between them there are workers that check the quality of the previous workers' execution of instructions and make corrections if they see it could have been better. One checking/correcting worker (I call them re-checkers) can handle (for me) no more than 4 previously completed workers. If more — it starts to drift.
And it's very important how the work with the database is arranged during the execution of the task, because the researcher can't do quality research if it holds and decides everything in its head
In the model's head everything starts averaging toward the mean denominator of everything that got in there
The model should look into the cells progressively, receive in the cell a contract for creation, do the work, and tick the box that the cell is done.
Then essentially research/copywriting/creative turns for the model into a coding task
It can change 450 files in a unique way for each file — so it can also complete 450 tasks uniquely at max reasoning.
